searchText: Hmm why don’t eth specs account for ecdsa recovery values 2, 3? yParity, v are always assumed to be 0, 1. To prevent transaction malleability attacks. See https://github.com/kadenzipfel/smart-contract-vulnerabilities/blob/master/vulnerabilities/signature-malleability.md You’re talking about s>n/2 i’m talking about q.x>n (r is made from q.x) So points at positive/negative infinity? Doesn't the ECDSA algorithm implicitly or explicitly ban them due to representaion issues? Even then, isn't the rate of occurrence exceedingly rare? (but not as rare as a hash collision) These are not infinity there is N curve order and P curve field x is always < P but CAN be > N: N < x < P The case is rare but can happen I believe it is to save a bit. I have little understanding of this but last time I checked it's infeasible to find such an example. 1 in 2^128 chance. In Ethereum, x is not allowed to be greater than the order, but ECDSA allows it. This makes recovery parameter 1 bit instead of 2 bits.
